newsitem.title: USA: Birth defects no higher for Gulf War vets children.
newsitem.headline: Birth defects no higher for Gulf War vets children.

text.p: Contradicting some veterans' claims, a study in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine found no evidence of increased risk of birth defects among the children of U.S. soldiers who served in the 1991 Gulf War.

The research "provides substantial evidence that the children of Gulf War veterans do not have an increased risk of birth defects," said the team led by Dr. David Cowan of the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research.

Using the records of more than 75,000 children born at military hospitals the team found the overall risk of any birth defect was 7.45 percent and the risk of severe birth defects was 1.85 percent. These rates are similar to those reported in civilian populations, the researchers said.

The study, based on Defense Department data, is likely to fuel debate over complaints by some Gulf War veterans who say they and their offspring have had health problems as a result of their serving in the war.

Cowan and his team said the research had limitations. Only children born in military hospitals were included and the team was unable to study children born after their parents left active duty or babies born to people serving in the military reserves. The study also did not look at the rate of birth defects in aborted or stillborn children.
In addition, it only measured defects apparent at birth. Defects that appeared later in life or were spotted in non-military hospitals or in outpatient clinics would have been missed.

But the Cowan team said the number of cases evaluated and the fact that no trend was seen when adjustments were made for race, ethnicity and marital status argued strongly that Gulf War service did not set the stage for birth defects.

People who served longer in the Gulf did not have a higher risk of parenting a child with birth defects, which the study took as another sign that Gulf service did not pose a risk. It also found no evidence Gulf War veterans had any fertility problems or that the sex ratio of their children was unusual.

So-called Gulf War Syndrome has been a topic of hot debate among veterans, especially after the Pentagon revealed that some troops may have been exposed to small amounts of Iraqi nerve gas. Those who believe they suffer from the syndrome complain of various medical problems including fatigue, sleep disorders, headaches and pain in the joints and muscles.

Last November the New England Journal published two studies of medical and death records showing no evidence that Gulf veterans fell ill at a higher-than-expected rate. At the time, Dr. Edward Campion, a deputy editor at the Journal, advised doctors to "resist the pressure to diagnose a disease for which scientific evidence is lacking" although he acknowleded that medical knowledge is imperfect.
